text: Reinforcement learning (RL), especially Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), has advanced model post-training in verifiable domains such as code and mathematics, where correctness provides a direct learning signal [ 46 , 16 , 50 , 75 ] . In contrast, evaluating video quality, especially emotional expression, often depends on subjective aesthetics and has no uniquely correct target. Visual post-training adapts diffusion and flow generators through RL and preference objectives [ 2 , 12 , 43 , 60 , 72 , 29 , 80 ] . Learned evaluators provide scores for image preference and video quality [ 69 , 22 , 38 , 68 , 17 , 30 ] , but a visually clear, temporally stable video can match its prompt without conveying the intended emotion. Facial analysis, dynamic expression recognition, and multimodal emotion models supply complementary evidence [ 1 , 3 , 7 , 26 , 79 ] , whose reliability varies with context: facial cues require visible faces, strong motion can undermine restrained sadness, and saturated colors may reflect style rather than emotional intent. This raises a central question: Which emotional evidence should the reward system trust in the current video, and how can it adaptively determine how much weight to assign to that evidence?

Agentic systems coordinate interaction, refine outputs through feedback, and organize evaluation into rubrics [ 65 , 62 , 39 , 47 , 15 ] . These capabilities motivate adaptive evaluation, yet existing video GRPO methods typically rely on fixed rewards for visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment that inadequately capture emotional intent. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and preference optimization address subjective goals [ 8 , 48 , 41 , 44 ] , but human annotation is costly at scale, and aesthetic differences complicate the calibration of emotional cues across contexts. Fixed fusion can mix informative, missing, and saturated signals, allowing policy updates to exploit scoring shortcuts rather than improve emotional fidelity. This motivates reward calibration at two complementary levels: assessing which cues are valid within each video, and learning from a completed training run how much those cues should influence rewards in the next run.

We introduce EmoReward , a self-evolving training mechanism for emotional video-generation RL (Figure 1 ). It distills evidence reliability from reward–outcome traces collected during an actual, completed training run, then uses this experience to guide multi-reward weight allocation in the next run to decide which emotional evidence to trust and how much to weight it. Plan translates emotional intent into an EmoScript specifying affect targets, facial and body cues, and an expression window; Act scores generated videos with heterogeneous primitives, keeping criterion scores separate from evidence validity. Within each video, Reflective Reward Gating calibrates these cues using the training phase, face confidence, semantic conflict, and subtlety, then renormalizes weights over active providers. After a training run, RewardMemory estimates provider reliability for each emotional regime from traces. Providers with stronger agreement are given larger weight multipliers for the next run, with limits on the size of the adjustment. These multipliers and all reward models stay fixed throughout that run; for each new video, reflection further downweights or excludes missing or unsuitable cues before the active scores are combined into a weighted average EmoReward can be integrated into several RL algorithms alongside general video rewards, and directly use training experience to calibrate reward allocation without retraining the evaluators.

We evaluate EmoReward on HunyuanVideo 1.5 [ 64 ] with DanceGRPO [ 72 ] , FlowGRPO [ 29 ] , and SAGE-GRPO [ 80 ] , observing higher VideoAlign scores for the guided configurations across all three RL algorithms on emotional prompts as the evaluation dataset for rollout. Under a fair comparison on the same RL architecture and training budget, EmoReward achieves the highest reliability selectivity and both composite calibration scores among seven reward policies. Ablation studies and mechanism analyses examine the contributions of reflective gating, provider pools, and RewardMemory (Section 4.2 ). Transfer experiments on Stable Diffusion 3.5 and FLUX show gains in selected configurations alongside objective-dependent trade-offs, while user studies show that EmoReward receives the highest human preference and proportion of Good ratings and the lowest proportion of Bad ratings for emotional fidelity, temporal coherence, and visual quality.

Our contributions are threefold. • We introduce EmoReward , to our knowledge the first self-evolving training mechanism for emotional video generation RL that calibrates reward providers across training runs without updating reward model parameters. • We propose RewardMemory , to our knowledge the first memory designed for multi-reward systems in video generation. It distills evidence reliability into bounded fusion weights, enabling iterative calibration of RL reward signals across training runs. • We inspire a novel cross-run self-evolution paradigm for post-training multimodal foundation models: a completed training run informs reward allocation in the next, making training experience reusable at the run level. Extensive experiments across three video RL algorithms and two image backbones, with ablations and human evaluations, validate EmoReward’s effectiveness.

sections.heading: From verifiable RL to agentic feedback for non-verifiable rewards.

text: RLHF learns subjective preferences [ 8 , 41 ] , whereas verifiable RL exploits correctness checks [ 16 , 75 ] . Agentic evaluators [ 77 , 9 ] and adaptive rubrics [ 15 , 70 , 78 ] structure open-ended feedback. Related approaches route experts [ 40 ] , refine responses [ 39 ] , evolve rewards [ 35 , 76 ] , or organize experience [ 47 , 71 ] . JitRL derives closed-form policy updates from retrieved action advantages [ 25 ] . EmoReward instead transfers reward–outcome evidence across completed training runs to calibrate frozen providers, combining sample-level gating with persistent fusion weights.

Agentic visual creation organizes generation into planning, tool use, and feedback-driven refinement. Video agents coordinate multi-shot narratives, script evaluation, audiovisual planning, and learned camera control [ 82 , 18 , 81 , 11 , 57 , 67 ] . Image agents combine knowledge retrieval [ 14 , 4 ] , learned creation and editing policies [ 23 , 27 ] , and experience reuse [ 5 , 6 ] . Other approaches jointly improve generation and evaluation [ 28 , 51 ] . EmoReward naturally achieves a self-evolving mechanism in video generation RL training, rather than building a workflow or retraining reward models.

Related 3D, audiovisual, and objectives for human animation address complementary aspects of visual generation [ 24 , 19 , 59 , 55 ] . Motion editing and transfer [ 52 , 54 , 37 ] , shape-aware and consistent image editing [ 33 , 36 ] , and pose- and identity-preserving animation [ 58 , 42 , 56 ] offer finer control over visual content. In this paper, we proposed EmoReward, a self-evolving reward calibration framework for emotional video generation reinforcement learning. EmoReward combines instance-level Reflective Reward Gating with RewardMemory, which transfers provider-reliability estimates from a completed training run to subsequent optimization without updating reward-model parameters. Experiments across video optimizers, complemented by ablations, image-transfer analyses, and human ratings, support the utility of adaptive calibration while identifying objective-dependent trade-offs. These findings suggest that completed-run experience can inform the allocation of trust among heterogeneous reward providers, providing a foundation for further research on reward-system evolution across training.

sections.heading: Appendix A Limitations and Future Work

text: EmoReward studies a training-adaptive reward system that transfers evidence about provider reliability between generator-training runs without updating reward-model parameters. The present evaluation focuses on emotion, where different scenes call for different combinations of facial, gestural, semantic, and motion evidence. A broader application would require a task-appropriate provider pool and a meaningful outcome for calibration. Action fidelity and audio–visual correspondence are natural visual extensions; language models and tool-use agents could similarly combine semantic judges, execution checks, and trajectory-level assessments. Whether the same calibration rule transfers effectively remains an empirical question, especially when providers share errors or outcomes favor only part of the task.

sections.heading: Appendix A Limitations and Future Work

text: A completed training run can be treated as a unit of experience for its successor. Repeating this procedure could produce a sequence of generators and reward-allocation tables, with each generation contributing new traces. Our experiments evaluate a reference-to-calibrated transition, not sustained improvement across many generations. Such an extension must address distribution shift, stale evidence, and feedback loops that reinforce a proxy’s errors. Retaining diverse historical traces and evaluating held-out outcomes would be important tests of whether repeated calibration remains useful.

sections.heading: Appendix A Limitations and Future Work

text: The trace representation also suggests a way to carry human assessments of a completed model into subsequent training. For example, a reviewer who finds movement too weak could request greater emphasis on suitable motion providers in the affected contexts; excessive motion could motivate the opposite adjustment. This would complement sample-level preference feedback with structured assessments of a model’s final behavior, translated into bounded changes to the next run’s reward allocation. Mapping subjective feedback to providers and regimes, reconciling different raters, and preventing compensating failures remain open design questions. The ordinal study reported here evaluates outputs; it does not implement this proposed feedback mechanism.
